newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentina's Menem blames protests on "subversion".
newsitem.headline: Argentina's Menem blames protests on "subversion".

text.p: President Carlos Menem, harking back to Argentina's bloody past, on Tuesday blamed "subversion" backed by political opponents for fuelling recent violent protests.

Menem was asked by reporters about social unrest at a time of 17 percent joblessness, but insisted the violence was the work of a small group of stone-throwing subversives who clashed with police, who used tear gas and rubber bullets.

"There are presubversive gymnastics in Argentina. They are in a state of germination," Menem told foreign correspondents, saying that was why police were "obliged to put an end to this type of situation.
"Some of these protesters are old subversives. They are defended by political sectors. There are even children," he said.
Military dictators from 1976-1983 waged a "Dirty War" against suspected leftist "subversives" in which human rights groups say up to 30,000 people disappeared.
Echoing military leaders, who sought to ensure that parents would keep their children clear of "subversive" activity, Menem said on Tuesday: "Parents, take care of your children."
On Monday, Argentine teachers held a nationwide strike to protest the death of a young woman at a weekend rally in the province of Neuquen that turned into a battle with police.
Teresa Rodriguez, 24, was on her way to work when she was shot in the neck during a battle between local residents backing a local teachers' strike and paramilitary police.

Tens of thousands held a rally in Buenos Aires to protest her death. Some violence was reported at the end of the rally when hooded youths ransacked the Buenos Aires offices of Neuquen authorities and smashed shop windows. Local news agencies said six people were arrested.
Witnesses and unions blamed Rodriguez's death on gendarmes flown to the oil towns of Cutral-Co and Plaza Huincul to break up a highway blockade by the striking teachers and locals.
Government officials blamed infiltrators from opposition parties for the riots.

Neuquen teachers have been on strike for a month against 20 percent pay cuts. They have been backed in protests by poor Neuquen residents in an oil-rich region where the state's sale of oil giant YPF five years ago left thousands jobless. The unemployment rate in that region is about 35 percent.
